# Install on Windows

How to install pysacd on Windows 11 from PyPI with no compiler, run its first commands, and,
for developers, build it from source with MSYS2.

**What was tested.** A stock Windows 11 Pro 25H2 (long paths off, standard user account) ran, on
2026-11-25: installing Python from python.org, `py -m pip install pysacd` with the 0.5.5 wheel,
pipx, `pysacd toc`, `pysacd-extract` and `pysacd convert` on a real disc image, and the source
build below with the fix branches of 0.6.0. The Windows on Arm wheel gap and an
organisation-managed PC (policies, redirected folders such as a OneDrive Music folder) were not
tried.

## Install Python

PyPI has one pysacd wheel for 64-bit (x86-64) Windows. It works with any 64-bit Python
<!-- facts:python-min -->3.10<!-- /facts --> or later, as it isn't tied to one Python version; CI runs it on Python 3.13. The wheel
carries the engine, libFLAC and mutagen, so nothing else is needed. There is no wheel for Windows
on Arm; there pip tries to build from source ([below](#build-from-source-developers)).

1. Download the Windows installer (64-bit) from
   [python.org](https://www.python.org/downloads/windows/) and run it.
2. On its first screen, tick **Add python.exe to PATH**, then choose **Install Now**.
3. Open a new PowerShell window (Start menu, type `PowerShell`) and check it:

   <!-- docs-run: skip="Windows: the py launcher exists only on Windows" -->
   ```powershell
   py --version
   ```

   *You should see* `Python 3.` and the version you installed.

## Install pysacd

In PowerShell:

<!-- docs-run: skip="Windows: PowerShell and the py launcher; the same pip install runs on Linux in install/README.md" -->
```powershell
py -m pip install pysacd
pysacd --version
```

*You should see* `pysacd` and its version, then how the engine was built.

Or, to keep pysacd apart from your other Python packages, install it with
[pipx](https://pipx.pypa.io/). Close and reopen PowerShell after `ensurepath`, then:

<!-- docs-run: skip="Windows: PowerShell and the py launcher" -->
```powershell
py -m pip install --user pipx
py -m pipx ensurepath
```

<!-- docs-run: skip="Windows: run in a new PowerShell window after pipx ensurepath" -->
```powershell
pipx install pysacd
```

To update later, run `py -m pip install --upgrade pysacd` or `pipx upgrade pysacd`.

## First commands

The commands use an SACD image (ISO) at `C:\SACD\album.iso`; type your image's path instead.
They write into the current folder, so start in your Music folder:

<!-- docs-run: skip="Windows: PowerShell and Windows paths; the same commands run on Linux in the README's Quick start" -->
```powershell
cd ~\Music
pysacd toc C:\SACD\album.iso
```

*You should see* `Disc:` with the artist and title, then a line per area and one per track.

Extract the stereo area to DSF files, as `sacd_extract` would:

<!-- docs-run: skip="Windows: PowerShell and Windows paths" -->
```powershell
pysacd-extract -2 -s -i C:\SACD\album.iso
```

Or convert it to FLAC, named and tagged from MusicBrainz:

<!-- docs-run: skip="Windows: PowerShell and Windows paths" -->
```powershell
pysacd convert -f flac C:\SACD\album.iso
```

`pysacd convert` reads its settings from `.config\pysacd\config.toml` in your user folder, if
that file exists; [converting](../converting.md) has the options and the naming templates.

## Windows file names

- `pysacd convert` always writes Windows-safe names: characters Windows can't use in a name
  (`<>:"/\|?*`) are replaced, as `--portable-names` does elsewhere.
- Disc titles that are Windows device names, such as `CON` or `NUL`, get a leading `_`
  (`_CON`), in `pysacd convert` and `pysacd-extract` alike.
- Two tracks whose names differ only in case get distinct files (`Intro`, `intro (2)`), because
  Windows treats them as one name. See [pysacd-extract](../sacd_extract.md) for the details.

## Long paths

pysacd writes files whose full path is longer than Windows' usual 260-character limit, such as a
long album title in a deep output folder, with no system setting. It opens every output (DSF,
DFF, FLAC, WAV, cue, XML, ISO copies and their temporary files) by its extended-length path
(`\\?\C:\...`), which has no such limit. Messages and logs never show that prefix. Releases
before 0.6.0, which fixed [#217](https://github.com/dsd-toolbox/pysacd/issues/217), fail on such a
path. On a stock Windows 11, 0.5.5 gave, for an output folder of 215 characters, `pysacd convert`
`[WinError 206] The filename or extension is too long` (exit 1, nothing written), and
`pysacd-extract` exit 255 with an `ERROR: ... .partial: No such file or directory` line. With
those releases, write to a short folder, such as `C:\Music`.

Some other programs can't open files past that limit. Those built for long paths can, once long
paths are enabled for the whole system. That is optional: Microsoft's
[maximum path length limitation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/fileio/maximum-file-path-limitation)
page describes the `LongPathsEnabled` setting. pysacd itself doesn't need it.

## Build from source (developers)

To work on pysacd, build the engine with MSYS2's UCRT64 toolchain. It links statically, so the
DLL needs nothing beside it and works with the normal python.org Python. You also need
[Git for Windows](https://git-scm.com/download/win) and [MSYS2](https://www.msys2.org/).

The steps use two shells, and each command runs in the one named. gcc is on the PATH of the
MSYS2 UCRT64 shell only; PowerShell can't find it, and the editable install fails there with
`can't ask the C compiler (gcc)`.

<!-- docs-run: skip="Windows with MSYS2; CI's portability workflow builds it" -->
```powershell
# 1. In PowerShell: get the source, root certificates for the download (see below), then the
#    scarletbook library the engine links (pinned, checked)
git clone https://github.com/dsd-toolbox/pysacd C:\src\pysacd
cd C:\src\pysacd
py -m pip install certifi
py tools/scarletbook.py fetch --target x86_64-pc-windows-gnu --dest build/scarletbook
```

Then open the **MSYS2 UCRT64** shell from the Start menu and run the rest there:

<!-- docs-run: skip="Windows with MSYS2; CI's portability workflow builds it" -->
```sh
# 2. In the UCRT64 shell: the compiler, then the engine
cd /c/src/pysacd
pacman -S make mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-gcc mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-pkgconf mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-flac
make                                          # builds src/pysacd/_sacdconv.dll
# 3. Still in the UCRT64 shell, so that gcc is on the PATH: a fresh python.org Python has no
#    setuptools, which --no-build-isolation needs
py -m pip install setuptools==84.2.1
py -m pip install -e '.[convert]' --no-build-isolation
```

If `pacman` stops with HTTP 429 from a mirror, set `ParallelDownloads = 1` in
`/etc/pacman.conf` and run it again.

To link a scarletbook library unpacked elsewhere, set `SCARLETBOOK_DIR` to its folder, with
forward slashes or backslashes. The build stops with an error if the engine would lack it.

A fresh Windows may not yet hold the root certificate GitHub's certificate chains to: Windows
adds such a root only when its own TLS client needs it, and Python's doesn't ask. The download of
the scarletbook library then fails with `CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED`. So on Windows the download
also trusts [certifi](https://pypi.org/project/certifi/)'s roots, as well as the Windows
certificate store (roots your organisation installs there keep working): `pip install` from a
source checkout or the sdist installs certifi for the build by itself, and
`tools/scarletbook.py` uses it when it is installed. If you set `SSL_CERT_FILE`, pysacd uses
that file instead of certifi's.

To run the tests from the source tree, `src/pysacd/_sacdconv.dll` must exist: `make` builds it
there, and the tests load the engine from `src`, not from an installed wheel. [Development](../development.md)
has the tests and CI.
